title: Mother's Day (Play, Snapshots)
tagline: J. B. Priestley’s comedy of exchange: two mothers swapped for a day to teach two grown children a lesson.

overview.intro: Mrs Pearson and Mrs Fitzgerald live next door: one is worked hard by her family, the other has an assertive fortune-teller’s manner and a plan. The plan is to exchange mothers for a afternoon and let the Pearson children discover what a mother is worth. The unit studies the mechanics of farce — the setup, the possession, the reversal — and the social argument underneath the laughter: Priestley’s comedy of manners is also a case about how families take kindness for granted.

learn.title: The setup: two neighbours and one problem

blocks.text: The play opens with an unusual pairing. Mrs Pearson is the accommodating mother whose family orders her about; Mrs Fitzgerald is a neighbour with fortune-telling experience and a blunt, assertive way of speaking, who regards the arrangement as intolerable. Their conversation supplies everything the audience needs — the children’s rudeness, the husband’s complacency, and Mrs Pearson’s habit of yielding — and Priestley uses it to establish the diagnosis before the treatment begins. The comedy is already present in the contrast of the two women: one apologises, the other commands.

The plan is proposed and agreed with the speed farce requires: Mrs Fitzgerald will exchange roles, or spirits, with Mrs Pearson, and for one afternoon the family will be managed by someone who does not care what they think of her. The audience accepts the device because the play’s interest is not the mechanism but the social experiment: what happens to a household when the person it ignores stops being obliging? The setup is the part of the play that examination answers most often compress, and it should be given its due — the problem is stated, evidenced and diagnosed in dialogue before any magic occurs.

items: Mrs Pearson endures a family that treats her as a servant.
Mrs Fitzgerald proposes the exchange with brisk authority.
The dialogue supplies all the exposition the play needs.
The device is farcical, but the question it poses is social.
The comedy begins in the contrast between the two women.

blocks.text: Once the change has taken place, Mrs Pearson — now speaking and behaving like Mrs Fitzgerald — proceeds to dismantle the family’s habits in a single afternoon. Cyril is told his smoking and idling will end; Doris’s complaints about suitors and dance partners are answered with a frankness that horrifies her; and Mr George Pearson, arriving with his usual assumption of entitlement, finds his pipe, his newspaper and his expectations of dinner all under review. The dialogue carries the whole reversal: the same mother, previously mute about her grievances, now speaks in clipped, contemptuous sentences, and the family’s confusion is played for laughter because they cannot locate the change.

The stage business matters as much as the speech. Cards, drinks, cigarettes and the tea-table are handled so as to disrupt routine — the family’s ordinary props become the objects through which the new order asserts itself — and Priestley’s directions keep the pace brisk, since farce depends on tempo. Underneath the laughter the mechanism of the comedy is precise: the family recognises the changed behaviour as wrong for a mother, which reveals that their idea of mothering consists entirely of service. The confrontation is therefore an argument conducted as embarrassment.

blocks.caption: The family confronted one by one
rows: Told plainly that the privileges will stop
Her foibles repeated back to her, unsparingly
Made to see his complacency in public

The exchange itself is the correction

blocks.text: The reversal is completed when the family, frightened and bewildered, is made to understand what has been happening, and the roles are restored — with the crucial difference that the restored Mrs Pearson is no longer the old doormat. The ending’s comedy depends on the family’s relief colliding with their new wariness: they have been shown what life without her compliance would look like, and they have not enjoyed it. Priestley’s technique is to give the audience both outcomes — the family repentant, the mother secure, the neighbour vindicated — so that the play closes on laughter rather than on lecture.

The message, stated through comedy rather than sermon, is straightforward: the people a household relies on should not have to be transformed into strangers before they are noticed. For examination purposes the ending supports a question about whether anything really changes. The generous reading is that the family has been taught a lesson it will remember; the sceptical reading is that they have been frightened into temporary good behaviour, and only Mrs Pearson’s new confidence will last. A strong answer takes a position and supports it with the play’s own evidence — the family’s relief, the mother’s changed tone, and the neighbour’s parting satisfaction.

learn.title: How a short play argues through comedy

blocks.text: Priestley’s method in this piece is economical: exposition in dialogue, one big device, character exposed through speech, and a reversal that restores order with a difference. Everything is compressed into a single afternoon, the set is a living room, and the cast is five — which means that each line must do at least two jobs, advancing the plot while revealing the speaker. Students should note how little is narrated: in drama everything is shown in the moment of speaking, and the mother’s previous misery is established entirely by what other people say about her.

The social argument is equally economical. The Pearsons are not villains; they are ordinary, and that is Priestley’s point — taking-for-granted is a family habit rather than a vice, and it is corrected in an afternoon by a neighbour who refuses to be polite about it. The fortune-teller’s trade is a pleasing touch of irony: Mrs Fitzgerald’s professional pretence at reading the future turns out to be an accurate reading of the present. Answers on theme should keep this irony in view, because it converts a farcical device into a coherent design.

questions.explanation: J. B. Priestley is the author; the play appears in Snapshots.

questions.explanation: Both are confronted in turn by the transformed Mrs Pearson.

questions.prompt: What does the transformed Mrs Pearson say to each member of her family?
questions.answer: She tells Cyril that his idling and smoking and his expectation of being served are finished, and that the privileges he takes for granted will stop; she repeats Doris’s complaints about her boyfriends and dance partners back to her with a frankness that leaves her speechless; and she lets her husband see that his assumption of dinner, his pipe and his evening silence will no longer be arranged around him. In each case she speaks plainly where the old Mrs Pearson would have accommodated them, and the family’s confusion comes from hearing their own behaviour described aloud.
questions.explanation: All three family members must be covered with the substance of what each is told.

questions.prompt: What is the message of the play?
questions.answer: The message is that a family should recognise what its mother does before she has to be transformed into a stranger for them to notice. Priestley shows an ordinary household — not unkind people, but people whose habits have made them blind to service — and the comedy exposes how completely they equate mothering with being obliging: their shock at the changed Mrs Pearson reveals that they never imagined her as a person with preferences of her own. The play also suggests, through Mrs Fitzgerald’s brisk intervention, that such blindness needs an outsider to break it, since the family would never have examined itself voluntarily. The lesson is delivered as laughter rather than as a moral, which is why it stays with an audience: the family is frightened into understanding rather than lectured into it.
questions.explanation: Three elements are required: the take-for-granted habit, the exposure of the service idea of mothering, and the outsider’s role in prompting the recognition.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley use comedy to argue about family life? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The argument is conducted through structure rather than speechifying. The diagnosis comes first and is delivered in dialogue: Mrs Pearson’s account of her family’s ordering her about, and Mrs Fitzgerald’s contempt for it, establish the problem — that kindness has been converted into expectation — before the device is even proposed. The treatment then works by inversion, and Priestley times each confrontation as a comic beat: Cyril discovers that his idling has been noticed, Doris hears her own superficiality quoted back to her, and Mr George Pearson finds that dinner, pipe and silence are no longer automatic. Because each character is confronted with their own habits rather than with an abstract principle, the audience laughs at recognition rather than at caricature, and the laughter is the argument: if the Pearsons seem ridiculous in their outrage, it is because their assumptions are common enough to be recognised in any living room. The stage business reinforces the method — the rearranged cards, the withheld tea, the interrupted newspaper are the visible grammar of a household whose service has stopped — so that the social point is made through objects the audience can see rather than through commentary. The resolution then applies the same principle to itself: order is restored, but not the old order, because the restored Mrs Pearson speaks with a confidence the family has just learned to fear, and the comic ending therefore carries a permanent change inside a temporary fright. Priestley’s own craft-note is the irony of Mrs Fitzgerald’s trade — a fortune-teller whose pretence reads the present accurately — which signals that the play is not a fantasy about magic but an observation about manners dressed as farce. The strongest answers will quote one exchange from each confrontation and show how the laughter it produces is aimed at the audience’s own habits rather than at the characters alone.
questions.explanation: Full marks require at least three comic episodes with quotations, the argument that laughter functions as recognition, and the observation that the ending contains a lasting change within a temporary fright.

questions.prompt: Does the ending change the Pearson family, or merely frighten them? Discuss with evidence.
questions.answer: The case that they are merely frightened is supported by the mechanics of the afternoon. The family never understands what happened: they cannot explain the change in Mrs Pearson, they react with confusion and panic rather than reflection, and their compliance at the end follows from relief that the ordeal is over. On this reading their good behaviour is strategic — they have learned that their mother can become someone they do not recognise, and they will be careful for a while — but no principle has been engaged, since a person who is startled into politeness has not understood why the original behaviour was wrong. The sceptical view gains further support from the form of the play: farce restores order by convention, and Priestley’s restored order is convenient rather than argued, so nothing in the text guarantees that the children’s habits or the husband’s expectations have been examined. The case that something genuinely changes rests on three pieces of evidence. First, the family’s own words at the confrontation show recognition: confronted with their behaviour described plainly, they are embarrassed rather than merely surprised, and embarrassment implies a standard they accept. Second, the ending does not return to the status quo — the restored Mrs Pearson keeps the new assertiveness, which means the balance of the household has shifted permanently even if the lesson is unspoken: the person they took for granted now has, and visibly exercises, the option not to oblige. Third, the presence of Mrs Fitzgerald ensures accountability: the family has witnessed that an outsider considers their conduct intolerable, and social shame of that kind tends to outlast a single fright. The balanced judgement is therefore that the fright is the method and the change is the result — Priestley uses alarm because persuasion would take a longer play, and the ending secures the mother’s position even if it cannot guarantee the children’s insight. An answer should hold both sides, cite the ending’s asymmetry (order restored but not identical), and end with a judgement about which change the text actually shows rather than which it hopes for.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both readings with textual evidence, attention to the fact that the restored order differs from the old one, and a judgement separating demonstrated change from wished-for change.
